memory_lessons.applicability: Large-input reductions using output zeroing followed by CTA-local accumulation and one atomicAdd per CTA.
memory_lessons.claim: The valid 2048-items-per-CTA/1024-CTA-cap candidate measured 7.72 µs, while the valid 8192-items-per-CTA/512-CTA-cap candidate measured 6.34 µs; both were correct on 10 cases. The baseline measured 46.67 µs. These measurements do not isolate whether the configuration difference caused the timing change.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this distinct 256-CTA cap configuration with the same correctness checks and repeated timing protocol.

proposal.hypothesis: The selected parent used up to 1024 CTAs and averaged 7.72 µs; a previous valid 512-CTA, 8192-items-per-CTA configuration averaged 6.34 µs. This candidate tests the opposite side of that tradeoff: cap the grid at 256 CTAs, increasing per-CTA grid-stride work, to see whether lower atomic contention outweighs reduced parallelism on large inputs. It is unmeasured; the controller should check correctness and repeated timings against both prior results and the baseline.

retained: For n >= 1<<20, launch output zeroing followed by the grid-stride atomic reduction on the default stream, preserving ordering.
Change the large-input grid to ceil(n/16384) CTAs capped at 256; keep 256 threads per CTA and one int32 atomicAdd per CTA.
Retain the existing hierarchical reduction for smaller positive inputs and explicitly zero the output for n <= 0.
